title: Why UX Researchers Undertrust AI Synthesis
stat: 88 percent of surveyed UX researchers call AI-assisted analysis the top trend this year, and 77 percent already use AI somewhere in their workflow
source: A published survey of UX researchers this year
topic_claim: the distrust of AI synthesis is the field's stated position
story_examples: One agent scanned four hundred papers and chose the twelve that counted as sources.
Another ranked a season of interview notes by strategic fit against our scoring sheet.
A third drafted the synthesis report before anyone opened the raw quote file.
thesis: That gap is why researchers distrust AI synthesis even when the output reads well: refusing to ship unverifiable claims is professional, not stubborn. The teams that keep access build differently, with traceable claims and counter-evidence on the record. Provenance gates, inspectable rationales, and a record of what got filtered before anyone looked are the specification
design_moves: put provenance gates in front of every synthesized claim
keep inspectable rationales on the record
counter: Researchers who refuse to hide the work are keeping the craft honest, and refusing to automate guards nothing on its own
definition: Epistemic access is a researcher's ability to walk backward from a claim to the evidence that holds it up
gap_stat_a: 61 percent of researchers trust AI to find patterns
gap_stat_b: only 47.6 percent trust it to turn patterns into recommendations
takeaway: Keep epistemic access inspectable: traceable claims, rationales on the record, counter-evidence surfaced by default.
question_tail: What would it take for your stack to pass that test?
person_context: I run agentic pipelines for research every week
